messages.subject: Seize a specific resource
parts:
I am modeling a customer service operation with 10 agents (add_resource("engineer", 10, Inf))handling a stream of tickets. New tickets are assigned to any available agent. 40% of the time that agent can resolve and close the ticket. In the other 60% the agent must request additional information from the customer and wait for that customer to respond. When the customer responds, the ticket becomes active again and must go back to the same agent.

 

In the trajectory below I think any available agent would be assigned the ticket.

 

How would I go about seizing a particular agent? Could this be handled using attributes?

 

cases <-

  create_trajectory("Resolve new Case") %>%

    seize("engineer", amount = 1.0) %>% 

 

  branch(function() sample(1:2, 1, FALSE, c(0.4, 0.6)), merge = c(F, F),

    create_trajectory("first day close") %>%

  # agent can close this case

      timeout(function() runif(1, 30, 60)) %>%

      release("engineer", amount = 1.0),

 

    create_trajectory("research/analyze") %>%

  # agent does research but will need more information from customer

  # do the research and send customer the request for information

      timeout(function() rexp(1, 0.0333)) %>%

      release("engineer", amount = 1.0) %>%

  # now engineer is now free but case is not yet resolved - wait for customer to respond

      timeout(function() rexp(1, 0.1666) ) %>%

 

  # repeat this cycle of steps a random number of times until the case is closed

  # roll back this trajectory and repeat with probability 30%

      seize("engineer", amount = 1.0) %>%

      rollback("research/analyze", amount = 1, function()sample(0:1, 1, FALSE, c(0.3, 0.7)))

) %>%

  release("engineer", amount = 1.0)

messages.author: 0f5b7adb7e70bd8b
messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] Seize a specific resource
parts:
First of all, a few things here:

  • The last release will be never executed because you set merge=c(F, F), and you don’t need it, because you release the engineer inside the branch. So it can be removed.
  • The rollback syntax is not correct. The correct one would be the following:
... %>%
  rollback(amount = 1, check = function() sample(0:1, 1, FALSE, c(0.3, 0.7)))
  • The rollback activity can climb up levels, so you can go back to the very first seize without repeating it inside the branch. That first seize is 4 hops away, so

cases <- create_trajectory("Resolve new Case") %>%
  seize("engineer", amount = 1.0) %>% 
  branch(function() sample(1:2, 1, FALSE, c(0.4, 0.6)), merge = c(F, F),
         create_trajectory("first day close") %>%
           # agent can close this case
           timeout(function() runif(1, 30, 60)) %>%
           release("engineer", amount = 1.0),

         create_trajectory("research/analyze") %>%
           # agent does research but will need more information from customer
           # do the research and send customer the request for information
           timeout(function() rexp(1, 0.0333)) %>%
           release("engineer", amount = 1.0) %>%
           # now engineer is now free but case is not yet resolved - wait for customer to respond
           timeout(function() rexp(1, 0.1666) ) %>%

           # repeat this cycle of steps a random number of times until the case is closed
           # roll back this trajectory and repeat with probability 30%

rollback(amount = 4, function() sample(0:1, 1, FALSE, c(0.3, 0.7)))
  )

And now, straight to the point: no, it’s not possible to seize a particular agent right now. But it’s an interesting problem. I need to think deeper about it. The first question is: is it statistically significant? I mean, seizing the same or not. Maybe it is, but it’s not clear to me. And if it actually is, I don’t see what’s the cleanest way to implement that.

Let me think about it.

messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] Seize a specific resource
parts:
You have a point there, Lindsay. Indeed, if tickets must go back to the same agent, it means that agents are distinguisable, so they must be different resources with their own queues. But the model grows linearly with the number of engineers. First of all, you’ll need one trajectory per engineer:

engineers <- sapply(1:10, function(i) {
  name <- paste0("engineer", i)
  traj <- create_trajectory("Resolve new Case") %>%
    seize(name, amount = 1.0) %>% 
    branch(function() sample(1:2, 1, FALSE, c(0.4, 0.6)), merge = c(F, F),
           create_trajectory("first day close") %>%

# agent can close this case
             timeout(function() runif(1, 30, 60

)) %>%
             release(name, amount = 1.0),

           create_trajectory("research/analyze") %>%

# agent does research but will need more information from customer
             # do the research and send customer the request for information
             timeout(function() rexp(1, 0.0333

)) %>%
             release(name, amount = 1.0) %>%

# now engineer is now free but case is not yet resolved - wait for customer to respond
             timeout(function() rexp(1, 0.1666) ) %>%

             # repeat this cycle of steps a random number of times until the case is closed
             # roll back this trajectory and repeat with probability 30%

rollback(amount = 4, check = function() sample(0:1, 1, FALSE, c(0.3, 0.7)))
    )
  result <- list()
  result[[name]] <- traj
  result
})

Then, you need a function to check all engineers and select the one with less tickets:

selector <- function() {
  which.min(sapply(1:length(engineers), function(i) {
    env %>% get_server_count(names(engineers)[i]) +
      env %>% get_queue_count(names(engineers)[i])
  }))
}

And finally, you need to put everything inside a branch governed by the selector above:

case <- create_trajectory("select engineer")
do.call(branch, c(list(case, selector, merge=rep(F, 10)), engineers))

And of course, you’ll want to add the resources to the simulation environment:

env <- simmer()
for (i in names(engineers)) add_resource(env, i, 1, Inf)

Nice one, uh? ;-)

​

Yeap, I understand the real scenario. What is not clear to me is that returning to the very same agent in the model, in the simulation, makes a real difference. Because in the simulation you have more flexibility, and you can, for instance, reduce the average research time for each rollback performed, thus simulating the experience gained.

If all your variables have the memoryless property (that is, exponential service times), then the identity of the agent is probably irrelevant. But this is only an educated guess. You can test both possibilities.

​
